After months of trying to get “big data” companies to disclose more about how they have manipulated the data on their clients’ devices in order to get them to spend more time on apps like Facebook and Twitter, the companies are finally doing it.
“Data privacy is increasingly a thing of the past,” the head of Apple’s privacy-focused Privacy Team, Susan Molinari, told CNET.
“There’s too much evidence that the companies do it without any privacy protections and that this is just how they do it,” she added.
But as the Guardian reported earlier this week, the data collected for Facebook’s Ad Library and Instagram’s Discover feature have revealed just how many devices are being used to spy on Facebook users.
And some of those devices are even being sold for a profit.
“We’re not disclosing this data to make you buy more apps,” Susan Molinari explained to CNET’s Sarah Harrison. “But we are going to make more money.”
At the moment, there are no publicly available records or court cases that have been brought against any of the more than 80 companies that have bought the data from the social media companies.
For now, the Facebook and Instagram data that’s been exposed is only available to a select number of people — and as the Guardian reported earlier this week, many of those people who purchased their data are still using those devices.
That’s the problem.
There are no legal protections for people in the U.S. who are using these services, and even if there are, the companies would be unlikely to enforce them anyway.
“We all know that the data that the companies are doing this with is essentially an intelligence operation. That is what they are,” Molinari said, adding: “The question becomes, is there a legal obligation to report this intelligence operation or is the right to privacy protected?”
As Harrison notes, “Facebook has been in touch with its users about the risks,” while, in turn, the companies are trying to put the best face on their situation.

Lerner touched off the public controversy when, at an American Bar Association conference earlier this month, she apologized for the IRS' practice of targeting conservative organizations for additional scrutiny. It was the first time the agency acknowledged the practice.
"They used names like Tea Party or patriots... and they selected cases simply because the application had those names in the title," she admitted.
She said she hadn't revealed the information sooner, because she was never asked. But just two days before the ABA conference, Lerner was specifically asked about the investigation.

Summary:
At a secret and confidential hearing Friday, the administration unveiled details of a massive, sweeping program to collect private information about communications from millions of American and international Internet users, calling it the Prism program.
The program was launched in 2007 by Mr. Clapper, a former deputy national intelligence officer for intelligence, and Mr. Obama’s national security adviser, James B. Clapper Jr., who was later fired.
This program was launched to give the administration officials greater control over the bulk data collection of Internet and other telephone records, in a dramatic change from the Bush administration’s approach to data collection. Officials said they had been trying for years to develop a program that would allow officials to obtain the information without judicial oversight.
For months, the administration resisted calling the information a data mining or program of any kind. Instead, officials insisted that it was a “transactional intelligence collection” program, which could be carried out “in an anonymous way” and without congressional approval.
But on Friday, the administration disclosed more information about its Prism collection program. For the first time, the administration revealed the name of the provider it uses to store the vast amounts of information.
“Prism” is an acronym for the program’s collection techniques. “Conducted in a public manner, the information will be made available to a national security entity,” the Justice Department said in its statement, which drew immediate criticism from some lawmakers who had never heard of the program.
The program would allow the collection of emails and telephone logs from the vast universe of American and international Internet users. Summary:
Obama's sweeping gun policy review is on the verge of becoming law
By MARK RALSTON
AP
June 24, 2012
A president on the brink of taking action on guns has a chance to send a message that his administration is serious about fixing a system that many in Congress say needs sweeping, sweeping change.
President Barack Obama has already put forward more than 2,000 legislative proposals to rein in gun violence. In all, about 2,000 legislative proposals to combat gun violence have been issued by the White House and the Democratic-controlled Congress.
The plan the president released Wednesday will be the strongest effort at gun control since President Ronald Reagan's.
In many ways, Obama's proposals are even more ambitious and far-reaching than previous government attempts to stop gun violence. This is likely because of the number of times the president is making proposals, and the sheer amount of work involved in the process. Obama was on a mission to make his administration a model for others. The Obama administration already has a huge number of executive actions that it says should all be implemented right away, including a proposal to require that all federal agencies report criminal histories to local police to help solve crimes. It also has dozens of proposals that it says could be immediately implemented, including new rules for the licensing and selling of firearms and ammunition.
But while the president is making these proposed changes, he is also sending them off to Congress to consider.
"The president wants to send these recommendations to Congress and the Congress will decide which of these recommendations it wants to pass on to the legislative branch," the administration's deputy spokesman, Josh Earnest, told reporters. "I'm confident that they're not going to agree to some of these proposals they don't like, even if there's some merit in it."
The president's plan also includes some significant changes to the way Congress is handling the funding of national programs to prevent and stop gun violence, such as school safety programs, mental health programs and the nation's gun trafficking laws.
The president's proposals on gun violence also have the potential to go beyond Congress by making major changes to how the federal government is spending its annual budget. The administration has proposed a proposal that would direct the Centers for Disease Control to start research on the causes and prevention of gun violence.

Title: Obama Gun Control Proposals Unveiled, Marking Biggest Legislative Effort In A Generation
Summary:
President Obama unveiled a plan today to enact a series of reforms to reduce the threat of mass shootings, including an assault weapons ban, a ban on high-capacity clips and federal funding to improve school safety. The president would be making his policy proposals during a "deep and broad" review of existing gun laws, Vice President Biden announced at an event in the Oval Office today.
"I want to be clear: this effort is not the end of it," the vice president said today. "This is an important step in this process. We are working hard on how best to reduce the likelihood of tragic gun violence, and that is why we are going to make this as comprehensive and robust a review as we can."
As with past policy recommendations, the president's proposals would require congressional approval.
A senior administration official confirmed to ABC News that the administration was not considering any new executive actions before it had laid out the full set of plans. The official spoke on condition of anonymity.
One senior administration official said the president will be working with Senate appropriators to put together a version of his proposal that could be used to shepherd it through a Congressional process, where the president has more weight. Another administration official suggested this plan may be a short-term fix to address a looming problem of mass shootings, while the administration is also weighing a proposal to address domestic gun violence.
A senior administration official said the administration's proposal does not address the national demand for stricter gun laws, but instead seeks to reduce "gun violence at the local level."
Under the proposals, the federal government would offer federal funding to states for "fire safety" improvements and for mental health training. The White House says the money would help cities and states to respond to mass shootings.
In addition, the administration is looking at federal spending to fund police departments to train officers on how to respond to active shooters.
"This is not about funding more cops, it's about more officers," the president said. "If you don't get your hands on the guns, someone else will."
The president's proposals also call for a federal gun trafficking statute, which he will ask Congress to pass. In his opening remarks, Biden called the proposal "one of the greatest public safety victories of our time."
"This is a step toward eliminating the risk of mass shootings in America and making our schools safer," Biden said. "By taking our children's lives and public safety seriously we can take this country to the next level, toward creating a safer and healthier nation."

By Amy Arar
WASHINGTON -- President Barack Obama on Wednesday laid out a sweeping plan to combat mass shootings in the country, drawing upon the administration's own top law-enforcement officials to push for better training, enhanced federal law enforcement, and a federal gun trafficking law.
"This is a moment of reckoning," Obama said in a speech highlighting the nation's gun laws, which he called a "burden" that will soon have to be met. "It is a moment of reckoning for all of us who want a government that is strong enough to provide for its people and protect its communities and its future."
Obama's proposal, which came at the end of a month-long review process spearheaded by Vice President Joe Biden, includes five pieces of legislation. The administration is recommending that the U.S. Department of Justice create a new federal gun trafficking law; create a federal gun trafficking task force to help the government enforce the law; require criminal background checks and gun sales records to be created for all gun sales; institute background checks for all gun sales; prohibit those in possession of firearms who are subject to a restraining order from buying additional guns; and require new mandatory mental health screening for those buying any gun from a federally licensed dealer. The cost of the plan, senior officials said, would be roughly $500 million, which may come from other federal funds.
The president will also recommend an expansion of the Federal Emergency Management Agency, creating an expanded position to oversee the disaster response; an increase in funding for school mental health programs; an end to the gun ban in some school districts; more funding for mental health treatment for law enforcement officers; greater support for public safety officers; and more resources for school security. The president would like to see the government commit more funding toward police officers, first responders and school officials.
The administration also recommends a package of 23 executive actions to take immediately to reduce gun violence. Republicans are challenging a host of statements made by Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and Democratic allies during Wednesday's heated Libya testimony -- claiming that complaints about a lack of funding are bogus and questioning the secretary's insistence she never saw urgent cables warning about the danger of an attack.
The questions come as the Senate Foreign Relations Committee begins its confirmation hearing for Sen. John Kerry, D-Mass., who was tapped to replace Clinton at the department.
One issue that may come up is the department's funding. Assertions that State Department posts are left vulnerable because Congress has decided not to fully fund security requests pervaded Wednesday's hearings.
"Shame on the House for... failing to adequately fund the administration's request," Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., said, after Republicans introduced legislation Tuesday that would require a confirmation hearing and an ethics investigation for the outgoing chief.
Clinton, in turn, affirmed their claims, saying budget issues are a "bipartisan problem."
Budget numbers, though, actually show the overall diplomatic security budget has ballooned over the past decade.
Democrats point to modest decreases in funding in recent years, and the fact that Congress has approved less than was requested. But Congress often scales back the administration's requests, and not just for the State Department.
And the complaints tend to overlook the fact that the overall security budget has more than doubled since fiscal 2004.
For that year, the budget was $640 million. It steadily climbed to $1.6 billion in fiscal 2010. It dipped to $1.5 billion the following year and roughly $1.35 billion in fiscal 2012 -- still far more than it was a decade ago.

Title: Obama Poised to Back Comprehensive Plan to Curb Gun Violence
Summary:
President Obama this week will embrace a comprehensive plan to reduce gun violence that will call for major legislation to expand background checks for gun purchases and lay out 19 separate actions the president could take by invoking the power of his office, lawmakers who were briefed on the plan said Monday.
Lawmakers and other officials said that the president could use a public event as soon as Wednesday to signal his intention to engage in the biggest Congressional fight over guns in nearly two decades, focusing on the heightened background checks and including efforts to ban assault weapons and their high-capacity clips. But given the difficulty of pushing new rules through a bitterly divided Congress, Mr. Obama will also promise to act on his own to reduce gun violence wherever possible.
Actions the president could take on his own are likely to include imposing new limits on guns imported from overseas, compelling federal agencies to improve sharing of mental health records and directing the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to conduct research on gun violence, according to those briefed on the effort.
White House aides believe Mr. Obama can also ratchet up enforcement of existing laws, including tougher prosecution of people who lie on their background checks.
At a news conference on Monday, exactly one month after the school massacre in Newtown, Conn., Mr. Obama said a task force led by Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr. had “presented me now with a list of sensible, common-sense steps that can be taken to make sure that the kinds of violence we saw at Newtown doesn’t happen again. He added: “My starting point is not to worry about the politics. My starting point is to focus on what makes sense, what works.”
The administration’s strategy reflects the uncertainty of gun politics in America and the desire by White House officials to address the Connecticut shooting while also confronting the broader deficiencies in the country’s criminal justice and mental health systems.

Title: Top House Republican Hints At Immigration Principles

House Republicans plan to release their immigration reform plan this week. But they aren't releasing it as a set of principles because they want to do it in pieces over the next two weeks, according to several people with knowledge of the plan.

Title: Representative Apologizes for Criticizing Iowa Senator
Summary:
This was another day in which politicians didn’t learn from the mistakes of others. It was another reminder that you never know which stories might prove to be the truth. A former lawmaker apologized, and now the guy who won an Iowa contest to be chairman of the Judiciary Committee.
— Karen Tumulty is the national editor of The New York Times Magazine.
— This story was first published in The Washington Post.

WASHINGTON — It is a lesson politicians never seem to learn from others’ mistakes: The microphone is always on.
The latest candidate to learn the hard way was Representative Bruce Braley, an Iowa Democrat running for Senate this year. Mr. Braley apologized to Senator Charles E. Grassley, Republican of Iowa, and “anyone I may have offended” after video emerged of him warning that “a farmer from Iowa who never went to law school, never practiced law” could become chairman of the Judiciary Committee.
Mr. Braley is not running against Mr. Grassley, who plans to seek a seventh term in 2016. But as the ranking Republican on the Judiciary Committee, Mr. Grassley could assume the chairmanship if his party takes control of the Senate this year. Mr. Braley, speaking at a January fund-raiser in Corpus Christi, Tex., was explaining why he should go to the Senate instead of his Republican opponent.
America Rising, a conservative political action committee that has vowed to use videos and opposition research to attack Democratic candidates, posted the footage on YouTube on Tuesday. Other Republicans quickly criticized Mr. Braley.
Though their numbers are declining, farmers are still a powerful force in the Iowa, which ranks second in the country in total farm sales. Mr. Braley’s apology noted his family’s history with Iowa agriculture, including his own stint “doing farm jobs and working a grain elevator.”
In another appeal to Iowa farmers, Joni Ernst, a candidate in the Republican Senate primary on June 3, announced in an ad that she grew up “castrating hogs on an Iowa farm.” Ms. Ernst said that qualified her to “cut pork” in Washington.

Overview of the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA)

In 2003, the US Congress passed the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA) to prohibit certain state laws that interfere with the free exercise of religion. Since that time, it has been the law of the land in all 50 states.

What makes the law even more potent, though, is that since 2003, the federal government has consistently allowed individuals to sue for federal protections under RFRA, and then only in extremely narrow cases.

What is the RFRA?

The RFRA protects people from being punished for practicing their religion. Religious individuals, corporations and other entities are protected from laws that deny them a fair shake in a marketplace. The RFRA says that the government cannot "impose a substantial burden on the exercise of religion," by making "government conduct a major factor in determining the regulation's effect on religious liberty," nor by "regulating conduct because it has the effect of burdening or restricting the practice of religion." The RFRA also bars the government from "invading the rights of a person by creating a classification of persons that either imposes an undue burden on such person or engages a fundamental transition of care."

The RFRA's purpose is to protect individuals from government interference in the free exercise of religion. It's not as controversial as it may seem, since the law is already in effect in all 50 states and more than 100,000 people have filed suit under it in the last 30 years.

A few weeks after he made his first major foreign policy speech, former Florida senator Marco Rubio on Wednesday outlined his foreign policy vision, describing himself as “missionally committed to taking America to the front lines of every conflict around the globe.”

"I am uniquely positioned to guide this administration, to ensure America is the global leader, when it comes to the military and our standing in the world," he said.

He was appointed to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee in 2010 by President Barack Obama, the first openly LGBT person to represent Florida.
Following his 2008 presidential campaign, when he won his first term in the Senate, he made the decision to run for the U.S. Senate against Republican Marco Rubio.
The two have been at odds since the 2014 election, and the race has polarized more liberal and conservative Republican groups.
Rubio has emerged as the frontrunner to win the race in the Senate primary held next January.

Title: Hillary Clinton's use of private email address while secretary of state draws scrutiny
Summary:
Former U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton used a personal email account to exclusively conduct official business during her time in the State Department, a move that raises questions about access to the full archive of her correspondence, as well as the possibility that she violated federal record-keeping laws.
The former secretary of state's decision not to have an official government email account appears to be contrary to records law, a former secretary of state under previous Democratic and Republican administrations, former New York City Mayor Mike Bloomberg and former Secretary of State Colin Powell, wrote in a letter to the Federal Records Advisory Committee.
"The Secretary should not have used a personal e-mail address, which has since been revoked by her, to conduct official government business," the letter reads. Title: Mike Huckabee on the Issues
Summary:
Former Arkansas governor Mike Huckabee has often been very outspoken. He’s taken some of these positions. But in this article, I highlight his stances on a range of issues. Here are his stances on important issues.

Mr. Huckabee warns that radical Islam is a grave threat to the United States and says President Obama too frequently defends Islam. He supports forceful military action against the Islamic State.

A strong defender of Israel, he has been sharply critical of Mr. Obama’s treatment of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and said a proposed nuclear deal with Iran is “terrible” because Iran cannot be trusted. Mr. Huckabee has talked of the possibility of using military force against Iran.

As governor of Arkansas in 2002, he called for lifting the economic embargo of Cuba, which would have helped rice farmers in his state. But he now opposes Mr. Obama’s warming of relations with Havana, calling Cuba’s government tyrannical.

In 2007 Mr. Huckabee was quoted as saying, “Climate change is here, it’s real.” But more recently he has minimized it as a threat, and said he opposes “cap and trade” legislation meant to curtail carbon emissions. “This kind of mandatory energy policy would have a horrible impact on this nation’s job market,” he said.

Mr. Huckabee says the immigration issue should not be treated as a federal issue. But he said Mr. Obama exceeded his authority by issuing executive actions shielding millions of undocumented immigrants from deportation. But Mr. Huckabee said the immigrant children whose parents brought them into the country illegally should not be deported because “you don’t punish a child for something his parents did.”

Mr. Huckabee is a strong defender of entitlements, opposing plans to raise the retirement age for collecting Social Security and criticizing plans to curtail Medicare. Republicans who back such changes, he said, “are embracing a government that lied to its people — that took money from its people under one pretense and then took it away at the time when they started wanting to actually get what they have paid for all these years.”

Chris Christie, as governor of New Jersey, has turned his hand to a difficult, but consequential, role. He has to run for the nomination, win the nomination, and then, in November, be the nominee again. So far, Mr. Christie doesn’t seem likely to convince the voters who chose a third party candidate to reconsider, or to become part of the Republican party. But he also doesn’t seem likely to get traction among the Democrats, who want a candidate who can beat Mrs. Obama. And for that reason, he’s the second most formidable of the third-party choices.
The other two third-party contenders — Paul Ryan and Newt Gingrich — are both very solid men and solid choices, but they also have very high debt loads, and they haven’t made money.
The only remaining candidate, Mitt Romney, might be the most plausible if he could raise enough money and run up big margins among the independent voters who vote in primaries in the United States — he may need to do so before he wins enough of those votes. The Romney-Ryan ticket is likely to choose their top two men early on in the primary campaign, and Romney is set to announce Tuesday the decision he's made about that next man. Title: Romney: My 'Preference' Is Marriage Between A Man And A Woman
Summary:
Mitt Romney on Wednesday said he wants a constitutional amendment that would prohibit same-sex marriage, but indicated he didn't rule out supporting a constitutional amendment that would allow civil unions to some people. His comment was made just hours after President Barack Obama gave a similar endorsement of same-sex marriage.
The news comes in reaction to Obama's announcement of his support for same-sex marriage that was given to ABC News on Wednesday.
At the same time, Romney said he would still oppose civil unions for same-sex couples.
"I'm still opposed to civil unions. I'm opposed to civil unions for same-sex couples, I am against civil unions for same-sex couples," Romney said in his interview with KDVR.
"But it is my view and as I said, that my view on that is that it is a question of states' rights. It is a question of our ability to control what we want to control. And I think that that is a state's decision."
While Romney said he would still support a constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage, he said he would support a federal measure to allow for civil unions in the country that had not been previously done.
"In this state, we could potentially go forward with legislation allowing that. And that is a decision that I think the states have to make. That is a decision that is ultimately for them to make. And I think I would be happy to support that as well," Romney said.
"But, again, what I have come to understand is that it is also up to the citizens of this country to decide."
The vice presidential nominee didn't elaborate on how he would go about creating such an amendment.

A vote is expected in the GOP convention in Tampa, Fla., this weekend to allow delegates to vote on a version of the party’s platform that would allow exceptions for rape and incest. If the convention rejects the plank, it sends a signal about the party’s stance on abortion.
The plan to limit exceptions for rape and incest has been championed by a small but vocal contingent of conservative Republicans, including Representative Michele Bachmann, and has emerged as a main rallying cry for many antiabortion Republicans, who believe that the party should not endorse an agenda that would make abortion harder to obtain.
Ms. Bachmann has vowed to vote against the plank if it is adopted.
“It would be a very irresponsible position for the party that we’re trying to take on this platform to be telling our citizens how we’re going to help them in terms of obtaining and keeping a full range of reproductive health and rights,” Mr. Romney said last weekend after a speech at the Family Research Council conference in Washington.
Mr. Romney is facing tough re-election fights in red states. Abortion rights may be one issue where Mr. Romney may face serious headwinds. His running mate, Representative Paul D. Ryan, is leading efforts in the Senate to end the nation’s abortion ban.

An idea that has become a rallying cry among House Republicans was that the House should try to replace Mr. Trump with someone else who, unlike Mr. Trump, can be trusted with power, such as Ms. Pelosi or another Democrat.

“Our founders saw that the chief executive had certain duties to perform and that these duties could be divided between the legislative branch and the executive branch,” Mr. Pascrell said.

WASHINGTON — The members trotted from their dugouts at Nationals Park, together in a near-summer air that never quite felt swampy, united in a certainty that the game must go on, just not exactly as it had before.
A day earlier, on another ball field some seven miles southwest, a gunman had opened fire on members of the Republican congressional baseball team, striking four people — including Steve Scalise, the majority whip of the House of Representatives — who were there for a practice.
And on Thursday, the capital’s various institutional forces — senators and lobbyists, staff members with a job to do and residents with an evening to spare — joined, for a moment, in a bipartisan rebuttal: Play ball.
Beneath a mostly cloudless sky, at least by the mid-innings, fans in the stands intermingled red and blue.
Near the dugout, the president’s daughter Ivanka Trump bantered with Chuck Schumer, the Senate’s top Democrat, who chatted with two of her young children. Nancy Pelosi, the House minority leader, wore a shirt from Louisiana State University, Mr. Scalise’s alma mater.
When a video message from President Trump played on the big screen, some of the Democrats in the crowd booed, but less lustily than usual.
“You are showing the world that we will not be intimidated,” Mr. Trump said. “The game will go on.”
Some members of Congress had not expected to stay behind for the annual showdown, with families and district business waiting for them.
But by nightfall, the decision was clear.
“We come here, and these members become our family,” Representative John Lewis, Democrat of Georgia, said at the Capitol before a game he had not intended to see.
He spoke of 1968 and of the political violence he had seen up close as a civil rights leader, invoking Martin Luther King Jr. and Robert F. Kennedy.
Mr. Lewis, now 77, stared straight ahead for a moment. “I have to stay,” he said softly.
All day, before as more than 24,000 ticket holders filed in for the charity game, the shorthand for other tragedies ricocheted through the Capitol.

Chief Justice John Roberts administered the 38-word oath at 12:00 p.m., capping Trump’s unlikely journey from New York City real estate developer and reality TV star to the nation’s highest office.

Title: Donald Trump Jr. Messaged With WikiLeaks During Presidential Campaign
Summary:

He exchanged several messages with WikiLeaks over the course of the year.
The emails between Trump Jr., who was a senior adviser to the campaign and also had a role in some of its foreign-policy and military-policy decisions, to WikiLeaks are some of the oldest in the public record.
In one, Trump Jr. appeared to refer to a Trump campaign video in an email exchange over the winter.
The next day, Trump Jr. sent an email in response to another email about a WikiLeaks video — but again, it was unclear how this was related to the campaign.
The emails show that between September 2016 and July 2017, Trump Jr. communicated with the WikiLeaks account more than 10,000 times. Most of the conversations centered on the campaign’s plans, but on some occasions, messages between the candidate and WikiLeaks are about the email account itself.
The exchanges are mostly about the Trump campaign’s operations, including its “tweet” account, which was set up to retweet pro-Trump messages.
After the presidential election in November, a spokesperson for the campaign told The Atlantic that the campaign had no knowledge of the messages sent to WikiLeaks, which the candidate said he and campaign officials had been trying to keep private.
The emails also have significant information about some of the president’s most important supporters, such as a member of the president’s legal team, Hope Hicks, who was in contact with the WikiLeaks account directly. She was also one of Trump Jr.’s closest advisers.
Weeks after Trump was elected, Politico Magazine published a book about Trump Jr.’s legal representation by his attorney Alan Futerfas that included many of the messages between the candidate’s son and the WikiLeaks account.

Summary:
National emergencies, such as national emergencies, can be declared in order to address an acute public safety concern or to respond to acts of terrorism or crime.
There are three common types: a declaration that would cause immediate, material damage or injury to the country; an emergency declaration, which would place a large emergency within the country’s boundaries; and a declaration that would provide a temporary relief from a legal or legal jeopardy in an attempt to end a dispute or bring about a desired outcome.
These three kinds of declarations involve different standards.
While a declaration that would cause immediate, material damage or injury to the country is the default setting in an emergency declaration, an emergency declaration would normally require only a declaration of temporary, limited emergency relief. A declaration that would provide a temporary relief from a legal or legal jeopardy in an attempt to end a dispute or bring about a desired outcome is considered to be of a more complex type.
Some types of declarations may not have immediate effects on the United States, but the government could make future use of the funds by issuing future regulations, legislation, licenses or permits.
There are a number of important exceptions and caveats to any declaration of emergency. It is not required, for example, that an emergency be declared if no damage is likely to be caused by the emergency itself or its potential effects.

House passed the Democrats’ showcase anti-corruption and voting rights legislation on Friday, an expansive measure that aims to dismantle barriers to the ballot box, end big money in politics and impose stricter ethics rules on federal officials.
Democrats used a series of gaffes and amendments to defeat a Republican effort to cut billions of dollars from the federal budget over the next 10 years by ending the annual spending of overseas troops at bases here or in the District, and by closing loopholes in the law that allow overseas bases to lease money from the Pentagon or their host country to pay for the troops’ salaries and overhead.
On Friday, Democrats tried an idea they’ve tried before and failed, but they hoped it would finally get traction in Washington: they used it in the House to defeat a Republican bill that would have ended the ability of foreign governments to award leases from the Pentagon to companies owned or controlled by U.S. citizens.
The GOP bill, sponsored by Representative Tom Graves of Kansas and Representative Chris Collins of New York, had included a provision that would have created a new federal agency, the Overseas Private Investment Corporation, to oversee such leases.
Mr. Graves, who called the proposal “vacuous,” said the GOP bill would have “fundamentally altered the structure of the Foreign Operations Appropriations Act.” He said lawmakers who wanted the amendment blocked were attempting to divide the caucus to create obstacles for Democrats who want to move forward on other legislation.
“Congress will not permit any members of Congress to undermine our constitutional system of checks and balances,” Mr. Graves said. “That is why this amendment will be defeated in the House today.”
And Republicans tried the same strategy to shut down another piece of their effort to end overseas military bases here. They accused Democrats of blocking the bill because they didn’t like the idea of allowing foreign countries to win lucrative leases to use facilities in the District without the Army and Marines’ oversight.
“Today, the House passed an important bipartisan piece of legislation that prevents foreign nations from using taxpayer money to rent space in the District of Columbia from government facilities to profit from our military,” said Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky.
Representative Thomas Garrett, chairman of the House administration committee, said the bill “has failed to live up to expectations.”
The bill passed 234-193.

Title: House Intelligence Committee Republicans Demand Chairman Adam Schiff's Resignation
Summary:
The House Judiciary Committee, Democratic-appointed committee chair Jerry Nadler, Intelligence Committee member Eliot Engel, ranking member Jim Jordan, and Republican-appointed committee member Devin Nunes sent a letter to the committee’s chairman, Adam Schiff, asking him to resign in order to restore the public confidence in Congress and its intelligence efforts. The letter, which has been signed by nine Republicans, accuses Schiff of creating a misleading narrative about the FBI’s special counsel, the investigation into Russian election meddling.
The letter demands that Schiff “immediately cease” public advocacy and “take the appropriate action to ensure that the full House has the authority to conduct the business of the American people,” including a special election to fill the vacant seat of a retiring Republican member.
Schiff told CNN that he planned on resigning.
As of Friday, a spokesperson for Schiff told CNN, “We will have no comment on the letters in question.”
In the letter, the committee members wrote, “It would be a travesty on your part to allow the false and misleading statements and attacks by Representative Adam Schiff (D-CA) to continue.”
The nine Republicans are also calling on Schiff’s leadership to “take immediate action” to remove him from committee oversight, as he reportedly has been working for a short time on a presidential “cleanup” of the Russia investigation.
“In your efforts to protect the President and shield himself from accountability for his actions, you appear to be using these committee members to do it,” the letter said.
In response to the letter from the lawmakers, Schiff said they are only asking for a few hours of his time, not his life, and they are not demanding he step down as chairman.
“We’re not talking about changing the leader of the committee,” Schiff told reporters.
Schiff’s committee has been under an intense fire since it was revealed that one of its ranking members, Intelligence Committee member Adam Schiff, is on the short list of potential 2020 contenders for chair of the House Intelligence Committee.
The California Democrat has kept the Intelligence Committee in the lead during the last two congressional terms, and has held the lead at the committee for more than a year.
With the panel currently set to focus almost entirely on the Russia probe in the run-up to its mid-term elections in 2019, Schiff faces growing calls to recuse himself from the committee.

It's easy to be negative about any bill that Congress passes.
As we’ve seen time and time again, lawmakers will fight to block even the strongest proposals to curb corruption and expand democracy. Some of those proposals were the most conservative elements of a massive spending and regulatory bill introduced by the Obama administration last year.
But Congress never does it alone. Even though it was bipartisan legislation, it still took weeks of negotiations and hearings to work through the details of the bill. This week, we’re taking a look at each of the bills passed by the House this past week.
The For The People Act (HR 3535)
By a vote of 234 to 193, the House of Representatives passed HR 3535, the For The People Act, on Friday.
The bill requires the creation of a federal election day holiday, which was not in the original plan, and creates the Department of Elections to handle the functions of voter registration. It would provide funding for state efforts to conduct and verify such registration, among other things.
It would prohibit partisan gerrymandering of congressional and state elections, but it doesn’t explicitly ban partisan gerrymandering. It also includes language that would prevent the Justice Department from acting on complaints that a state’s boundaries have been “discriminatorily drawn” based on certain political affiliation.
The bill would repeal the “gag rule” that prohibits members of Congress from speaking on a government-funded TV program. It also makes it easier for small donors to contribute directly to members’ campaigns.
The bill would amend the Federal Election Campaign Act to include the option for independent candidates to accept no contributions from labor unions.
House passage of HR 3535 is one of the landmark pieces of legislation the Democrats have worked on in the last month. It is one of the bills that would help fix our electoral system and ensure democracy. If Democrats have not accomplished so much within weeks of an election, it was a big win.
It was a win that would make a difference in the lives of millions of people, including in California, where a majority of the vote was for Proposition 30. Title: House Democrats Pass Landmark Campaign Finance And Voting Rights Reform Bill
Summary:
The House vote passed the bill 234-193 on Friday. The For The People Act requires public funding of elections for all House elections, expands voting rights and lifts ethics rules for the administration of federal affairs. It also introduces the Independent Money in Politics Oversight Commission, which would be tasked with determining whether money in politics is “fairly and equitably distributed.” It would also restore voting rights to millions of ex-felons in states that have abolished them.
The bill would also expand access to federal student loans, including increasing the $5,000 cap for Pell Grants. It also reauthorizes the Violence Against Women Act, includes voting rights for some veterans and extends the Violence Against Women Act to a new year. It also includes voter registration and other tools for expanding voting access, such as allowing states to implement new models of election financing that are more competitive and transparent.
It would give an additional $30 million in federal funds to states for public elections, including up to $30 million in federal funds for the first time in state elections. The federal budget would be used to pay for some of the costs of a state-based voter ID system, and for matching grants to state elections departments to help ensure elections are open and fair to all voters.
The bill restores voting rights to “all persons” who served in the armed forces. It also prohibits partisan gerrymandering, and restores “the right of suffrage” to all who are “exercised by any State or political subdivision thereof,” including ex-felons.
The bill “creates a federal election day holiday to celebrate the anniversary of the Declaration of Independence,” Rep. John Lewis (D-Ga.) said.
“This vote is an opportunity to be on the right side of history,” Lewis said.

The For the People Act (H.R. 2958) that passed the House 234-193 on Friday takes power from the elites, special interests and the 1% and gives it to the American people, which means all people, regardless of their race, their gender, their religion, their ability or lack thereof.

The bill aims to answer rising attacks on voting rights from courts and politicians across the country, and also to stem the increasing inequality of campaign funding by empowering small donors with matching contributions from public funds, among many other things.

Title: House Democrats Pass Landmark Campaign Finance And Voting Rights Reform Bill
Summary:
The For the People Act, which passed 234-193, was Democrats’ top priority upon winning control of the House in the 2018 elections. It would dramatically expand voting access, create publicly funded House elections, enhance the transparency of money in politics, restore voting rights to millions of ex-felons, strengthen executive branch ethics law and end partisan gerrymandering.

Summary: Democrats are working on a landmark bill to give new voting rights to millions of ex-felons.

The House of Representatives passed a major bill on Friday to boost campaign financing transparency, increase transparency on the role of money in politics, strengthen the transparency of lobbying and help those facing ex-offender re-entries and parole hearings.

On Capitol Hill, Republicans have been clamoring to have their own reform package introduced, and Democrats have long been opposed.

But Rep. John Sarbanes (D-Md.) helped craft the For the People Act, a compromise that would expand campaign financing, ease campaign finance restrictions and create new public offices for reform. While a handful of Republicans have introduced their own reform bills, they have stalled in the House after finding the political will for change, largely because the party controls the House majority.

That’s now changing as Democrats gain back control of the House, and they’re not just going after GOP efforts in Congress. Their agenda includes their party’s campaign finance, ethics and voting rights reform bill. It passed the House 232-193.

In a sign of the changing mood among House Democrats, several of their senior colleagues signaled on Friday that they support the For the People Act, a bill that would create new public funding of elections, expand voting rights for ex-felons and enhance transparency of campaign financing, among many other things.

The House vote on Friday was a compromise between those on the right and left, but Rep. John Sarbanes (D-Md.) helped draft the bill, which was backed by the Democracy Reform Task Force, a congressional group whose members include Democrats from across the country.

“We need a new system. We need a system that works,” Rep. John Lewis (D-Ga.) said ahead of the vote.

Title: House Democrats Pass Landmark Campaign Finance And Voting Rights Reform Bill
Summary:
The For The People Act was introduced as part of the Democratic Party’s reauthorization of the Civil Rights Act. It aims to expand voting access, make it easier to enforce voting rights, restore access to public funds for elections, create a public election board and end partisan gerrymandering.
This summary does not reflect the full content of the bill. For the complete text, see the bill, which the Government Printing Office website provides.
Key amendments that passed the House on Friday:
Amendment A (McConnell): Amends the Civil Rights Act to ensure that the United States Civil Rights Commission (the commission) has exclusive jurisdiction to investigate potential civil rights violations.
Amendment B (McConnell): Eliminates the right of certain noncitizens to run for office unless they are in the United States or United States-Confederated States of America, Guam or Puerto Rico, and grants citizenship to qualified foreign-born citizens.
Amendment C (McConnell): Provides for an additional 10-year period during which a voter-registration deadline can be extended, up to one year.
Amendment D (McConnell): Grants federal court injunctive relief in civil rights cases.
Amendment E (McConnell): Clarifies that the commission must issue the civil rights advisory opinion by Nov. 20, 2019, to be effective 30 days after the advisory opinion becomes final.
Amendment F (McConnell): Directs the commission to provide an additional one-page written summary of its findings and conclusions. The commission should also make the document publicly available on its website.
Amendment G (McConnell): Establishes that any federal court or agency order issued within 60 days of a court or agency ruling or any subsequent executive action is final.
Amendment H (McConnell): Clarifies that the commission shall issue an additional two-page written summary of its findings and conclusions, and shall submit the report to Congress by December 15, 2019, on December 22, 2019.
Amendment I (McConnell): Requires the commission to issue a second civil rights advisory opinion if an advisory opinion was not issued on or before Nov. 23, 2019, and to provide an annual update to Congress in the first quarter of 2020.
Amendment J (McConnell): Creates an 18-member independent commission to evaluate all existing federal civil rights law.
Amendment K (McConnell): Authorizes an election day holiday in certain states, to be made effective if the Senate does not adopt the bill.

When asked about the allegations that he has worked to collude with Russians, Stone said, "I think you want to make an election year mistake," and added that he didn't "know whether that's going to result in a perjury charge or not." 
CNN then showed Stone's interview with CNN and the grand jury indictment. Stone, who is being held in the Polk County Jail in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, was released from custody Friday after posting bail of $25 million.

A court appearance was scheduled for Friday morning. 
A judge also set a bond of $1.6 million for Stone’s two dogs, the Miami Herald reported. Stone’s attorney told the Herald that Stone “has zero criminal record.”

The House, in the 112th Congress, was the first to recognize that the Constitution had a purpose. By doing so, the Congress made clear in what it had in mind. “The Congress of the United States, in order to exercise the powers vested in it by the Constitution, may do one of two things”

Congress has the power under the Constitution to “do one of two things.”
Or it has the power under the Constitution to delegate that power to the executive branch.
In the House’s resolution, a distinction is drawn between the two powers, but that distinction does not seem to make a difference with the votes.
Either Congress can delegate the “power” that is included in the Constitution to the executive, or Congress can delegate “the power” that is in the Constitution.

“Congress may do one of two things”

Which does not require the Senate, or the executive branch, to agree.
It is the House that can decide.
If there is a majority in the House that does not support what the Congress says, the Senate must come into the House and ask the members what the majority wants.
If the Senate accepts the majority position, it becomes law.

Title: Supreme Court Questions Claims in Sex Bias Suit Against Wal-Mart
Summary:
A pending class action lawsuit against Wal-Mart that could be the largest of its kind in U.S. history could soon be dismissed, considering the tenor of oral arguments before the Supreme Court Tuesday.
Although she may ultimately side with the plaintiffs, even Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg expressed some concerns about the particulars of the sex discrimination lawsuit that covers 1.5 million women and could cost the world's largest retailer billions of dollars.
The key vote for a Wal-Mart victory could belong to Justice Anthony Kennedy, who said he was troubled by what he called an inconsistency in the women's lawsuit.
"Number one, you said this is a culture where Arkansas knows, the headquarters knows, everything that's going on," Kennedy told lawyer Joseph Sellers who represents the women. "Then in the next breath, you say, well, now these (local) supervisors have too much discretion."
The lawsuit alleges that the company's corporate culture, described in court Tuesday as the "Wal-Mart Way," fosters the advancement of male workers over their female counterparts. It also claims that despite a company policy expressly prohibiting discrimination, local store managers are given too much flexibility in determining salary hikes and job promotions that invariably favor men over women.
This dual argument that confounded Justice Kennedy also drew the ire of Justice Antonin Scalia who said he was whipsawed by the claims. "If somebody tells you how to exercise discretion, you don't have discretion," he said.
Chief Justice John Roberts also offered his doubts about the merits of lawsuit, suggesting that any discriminatory acts at Wal-Mart are no worse than anywhere else.

Title: House Republicans Read Constitution On Second Day In Power
Summary:
The House will vote Thursday on a number of bills with the intent of increasing the power of federal government. In the event this happens, it would not be the first time the Constitution has been read in full during the first day of the new congressional session. This is a very positive first step.

How it works
Read the articles and the amendments from the Constitution of the United States of America in their entirety, without reading through any of its sections or paragraphs, or skipping any of its references, and compare them to your own understanding of the text and its significance.
You must answer honestly if you believe that the article(s) and/or amendment(s) in any given case are a direct violation of, or in opposition to, the Constitution and/or laws of the United States, and you must indicate what is your reason(s) for being so convinced.
Note: Articles and Amendments are given according to their order of inclusion, and not in any particular order. The same cannot be said for the President’s orders, which he sends to Congress as part of the Articles of Impeachment, or the decisions of the Supreme Court of the United States on the same subject matter.
You are allowed to change your mind.
Note: It is difficult to compare the wording of the Articles and the Amendments to other documents. The American Experience, as written in 1812 by Thomas Jefferson, is the primary reference; and because of the difference in English syntax, it is difficult to match the text to any other document written in another language.
To help you make the most accurate decision you can, choose your favorite document, and compare it to your understanding of what the text says, and to the interpretations that others have made of it.
This will give you an estimate of the cost and benefit of each decision.
Your results are noted on a scale of 1 to 5:

1 - Never a good idea.
2 - Quite worthwhile.
3 - Quite worthwhile.
4 - Quite worthwhile.
5 - Very worthwhile.

The Constitution
Read the “Bill of Rights,” and find out which amendments and article(s) in the Constitution of the United States of America protect your rights as a citizen and/or a federal employee.

Title: Purpose Behind Congressional Reading of Constitution Questioned After Amendments Are Omitted
Summary:
The Supreme Court has ruled the Affordable Care Act in the federal health insurance exchanges to be unconstitutional. That means any future federal health plan must cover essential health benefits, including mental health care for people with substance abuse problems and care for the sick.
The decision is likely to send insurers scrambling to find new ways to offer medical coverage. It will also help the federal government make money from selling insurance across state lines through the newly created Healthcare Exchange.
The ruling may also help keep plans open, which is good for businesses, but bad for the federal government.
Congress is also reviewing new federal regulations that expand the types of medical coverage people can buy. For example, the new coverage is for anyone with preexisting conditions or who has lost their employer-sponsored insurance. This would include plans for people with pre-existing medical conditions.
And there are other changes.
The Obama administration had asked the court to uphold the law's mandate to buy health insurance, which requires individuals to buy the individual and small group insurance plans on the individual health insurance exchanges under the health care overhaul.
But the high court said the tax subsidies are required by the law to help people afford coverage. The court said the mandate is constitutional. That's an important win for Obama, who has struggled to find consensus on major reforms.
The decision could also help Obama in his quest to get Americans insured for long-term care, which is now a required part of Medicare. The Supreme Court said the Obama administration did not have to comply with the law to get the Medicaid expansion, which gives states the option to expand Medicaid for low-income citizens.
But the high court also said the Medicaid expansion would not be constitutional if the federal government was in charge.
The decision to rule the law unconstitutional comes on the heels of a recent Supreme Court decision by Justices Anthony Kennedy and Clarence Thomas that upheld the Affordable Care Act.
The court was the first to hear the case since it was brought before the court by the Obama administration, which said the law violated the separation of powers and the U.S. Constitution.
For those who still believe Obamacare isn't going to be overturned by the court, we asked White House spokeswoman Jennifer Psaki to give us her thoughts on what the president's message to the justices was.
"I want the American people to know that we, the president, have confidence in the integrity of the court," she said in a statement. "I am confident the Supreme Court will decide the law's constitutionality with the administration's support."

Article II, Section 1 (1844) empowered Congress "to make all laws which shall be necessary and proper" to carry out a president's constitutional duty.
In the late 18th century, Congress enacted and the state legislatures ratified amendments to the United States Constitution to give Congress the power to "redress" for its use or otherwise amend the Constitution. Article V of the Constitution created the House of Representatives with the President as Commander in Chief.
The original Constitution allowed Congress to "discharge its various duties," including enacting amendments, but never ratified an amendment. To qualify for ratification, it had to be either enacted or ratified by three-fifths of state legislatures. However, all three-fifths of the states ratified the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA) in 1986 to update the Constitution.
The ERA proposed an amendment replacing the word "natural" with the word "human." Although that amendment never made it into the Constitution, Congress included its original provisions for a two-thirds vote in the House and Senate and the ERA's language in the Constitution.
In 1954, Congress passed a joint resolution that amended the Constitution to require a two-thirds vote in the Senate and a two-thirds vote in the House to amend the Constitution. By a unanimous vote in each chamber, the ERA was ratified.
The ERA was ratified in response to the increasing number of women taking the role in politics. In 1976, the ERA passed the House and Senate by a large margin as a result of the increased percentage of women in the voting electorate.

Title: Bachmann Cover Controversy Prompts Response From Newsweek
Summary:
The Daily Beast’s decision to run a story about Ms. Bachmann’s “queer” antics is not without precedent. Last month, Newsweek ran a story titled, “Sexist Cover: Newsweek Pushes Queen For ‘Sexist’ Magazine Cover.” The piece included a picture of Ms. Bachmann and said she would be “emboldened” to “steal a few minutes of your time” during a Republican presidential debate.
In 2006, Newsweek ran a photo of then-Senator John Kerry with a caption, “Kerry In ‘Sexist’ Magazine Cover,” followed by the caption “Kerry in Sexy Shirt.”
There are also examples from the left that Newsweek has not always dealt with gracefully. In 1998, when Newsweek ran a “Hush-Hush” photo of former Vice President Al Gore, Gore took the picture of him looking out of his dark glasses and wrote on his face “Sexist.”
“Sexist” was also used as a title for a story that began, “It is alleged that Sen. John McCain once called Vice President Dick Cheney a ‘moron.’” In the article, Gore’s son, Beau, wrote, “‘We do not need any more of that John Kerry/Dick Cheney ‘stain.'”
That story ended up in a magazine that often seemed to find the most politically-correct image, but the headline of the piece, “’Sexist’ Cheney” was seen by many readers to be a play on, “Kerry” and “Dick Cheney.”
Newsweek has a history of being willing to be politically-correct. When Time magazine published an issue, in 1979, with a picture of Al Gore with the caption, “Sexist” and “Sexist Magazine Cover,” some women began to speak out.
The editor-in-chief at Time, Janet Cooke, apologized for publishing such an offensive photo. But the magazine never covered the story.
But last week Newsweek released the first photos from the interview with Ms. Bachmann in a photo spread in the current edition of Newsweek.
“The author of this report was not an active participant in the discussion and does not endorse the opinions expressed therein.”
So there you have it.

Newsweek is one of many news organizations out there that regularly, routinely publish the photographs of celebrities on their covers to create the illusion that they are somehow still alive. (See above.)
The Atlantic Wire story quotes a Newsweek editor as saying, “We do not want to make the image of someone who’s still in their life any less lifelike, so we would like to preserve as much of it as possible. And then we make it seem that the photographer is still there, that his shot of the celebrity is what’s going on, because that’s what makes the picture more attractive to us.”
The Atlantic Wire article also quotes a Newsweek editor as saying, “One of the great things about doing this kind of work is that it doesn’t come with the baggage of fame. If you’re famous, it’s easy for people to say, ‘This is me — this is me on my death bed — I can’t possibly look at your photo.’ Whereas here, it’s not, ‘This is me’ — it’s, ‘This is the cover shot that I had when I was famous.’”
This is not the first time Newsweek has made controversial editorial choices.
In March 2001, Newsweek put on a cover of the then-presidential candidate John Kerry in what was described as a “glamorous red dress,” and featured the first images ever of Princess Diana to be photographed by the famed photographer Cecil Beaton. (See the Atlantic Wire story above.)
The cover photo of Beaton featured his famous black-and-white photos of Queen Elizabeth II. (See above.)
The cover photo of the two princesses in the same scene created controversy. The photo was later removed and the original shot placed on the front cover — a photograph of Diana’s face on a white background.

Title: AARP Open to Social Security Cuts
Summary:
This article includes a transcript and an additional view on how Social Security benefits are affected.

It may be the first time in history that the members of one organization are going to have to answer to the public about whether or not Social Security benefit cuts should happen.

In addition to having the biggest lobbying influence for the Older Americans Act (OAA) group, AARP’s membership has long been seen as one of the most outspoken critics of Social Security reform.

The AARP membership has also long been a key swing vote on whether or not Social Security should be reformed, as well as advocating for changes in Medicare, prescription drug spending and other areas that impact the finances and needs of today’s retirees and future generations.

AARP has been on the receiving end of the ire from both sides of the debate over Social Security.

The idea of reducing benefits would seem to be both radical and unpopular, especially for those already struggling to keep up with rising costs from Medicare, prescription drug spending and other areas.

“I was surprised that AARP didn’t change its position on whether Social Security benefit cuts would be considered,” said Michael Stokes, president of AARP. “The AARP position of saying that cuts will be minimal is not changing from what it has been for decades.”

The AARP statement that it will consider further cuts in benefits comes after the group’s membership has been sharply divided as President Obama, congressional Republicans, even some Democratic senators, have made their own proposals for how to pay for the program’s proposed cost cuts and other reforms.

In April, the president proposed cutting the benefits for a third of retirees to help pay for tax increases; the White House was met with backlash from his own party, which criticized him for suggesting those cuts are a way to balance the budget.

Social Security benefit cuts are also a priority for a smaller group within the OAA group, who are pushing for changes that would reduce benefit amounts for current retirees.

In doing so, the organization has made clear its willingness to work with Congress to make the benefits system more solvent, despite its stance on possible cuts.

Title: Did Ruth Bader Ginsburg Cross The Line With Her Donald Trump Comments?

We can expect Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg to soon be the fifth and maybe the fifth in the last five years to comment critically on Donald Trump in an interview with The New York Times.

The liberal-minded judge's comments are well known, but there is another side to this story, which is more than a little ironic.

After all, Ginsburg was a justice at the same time that the first woman ever to have her name put on an official stamp of approval in our courts came into being.

What makes this point more disturbing is the fact that Ginsburg has been in the limelight recently for no reason other than she has been deemed (to use a more colloquial term) "political."

It should come as no surprise to anyone following the judicial proceedings at all that she has commented on a number of things that were said about the president, mostly with no consideration of the political ramifications.

A good example:

The comment: “Well, it’s not only the president of the United States that you say is in denial of reality, but I think it’s been said that he is also in denial of reality.”

The article: “In another court interview, Ginsburg also weighed in on one case. ‘This is so silly,’ she said. ‘You don’t have to explain it.’ ”

The reaction of the New York Times: “The decision was greeted with approval. The Times described it as ‘a nice change of pace for Ms. Ginsburg, who has said a few bad things about Trump.’”

The article continues: “Ginsburg was asked whether she still agreed with what she said earlier in the day about Trump’s denial of climate change. ‘I don’t think so,’ she said.”

Why? It's easy to see why. First of all, we can't know how many other justices would agree with what she said. Second, this is part of the process, and we can't expect the people with the power to make those decisions to comment on every single decision of the court.

We could ask Justice Samuel Alito, or Justice Clarence Thomas, for example, but their opinions are not public; the articles do not say anything about their reasoning; and there is a public record about how these opinions came to be.

Title: For Trump and Bloomberg, Cordial Ties Have Soured
Summary:
Donald J. Trump and Mike Bloomberg have had more than one run-in over the years. From the first days of New York’s mayoralty and into the fall of 2017, the two men would argue about each other and their politics. But in the end, it was neither one of them who was the more loathsome of the two.
Mr. Bloomberg is a former financial titan who, from his own admission, did not like the idea of Mr. Trump as mayor. On the other hand, Mr. Bloomberg’s daughter Georgina, while not in favor of his candidacy, is very much in favor of Mr. Trump’s. Mr. Trump does not always give Mr. Bloomberg the credit he deserves.
Mr. Bloomberg spent much of the 1970s building a fortune on Wall Street. Then his fortune was pared and the money he made into his foundation was put into his various projects, which he spent lavishly.
He has always been generous to charity and the arts. He did not want Mr. Trump as mayor. But on the Trump candidacy, he tried to make it difficult for Mr. Trump to win, and to keep Mr. Bloomberg out of it.
Mr. Bloomberg gave Mr. Trump, despite his reputation as a “dog-eat-dog” candidate, the benefit of the doubt. When the media reported that Mr. Trump had not paid his campaign debts, Mr. Bloomberg said he had no comment, and he kept a promise to himself to keep the Trump campaign from being his biggest campaign asset.
Mr. Bloomberg also did not want to run against Mr. Trump in his second term, so his campaign committee ended up backing him to win. When he ran for president, he pledged to back him and support him, and now he appears to be backing him out.

Summary:
Obama and Clinton are fighting a political battle in the middle of a terror attack on a gay nightclub.
President Obama was briefed early Sunday, prior to the attacks, by Vice President Joe Biden, and White House officials said the administration did not consider the attack a terrorist attack.
“The president is fully prepared to take action as appropriate, and that action includes the continued support of our law enforcement agencies on the front lines of this investigation,” Obama said in a statement. “The president will not hesitate to do so if there is additional information to indicate a terrorist motive.”
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security said on Twitter that “all federal agencies are responding to the attacks in Orlando, Florida and are assisting local law enforcement.”
Obama and Clinton have also been calling on the federal government to spend more resources on security.
“All agencies are fully committed to ensuring the safety of all Americans and the people of Orlando, Florida,” Obama said Sunday.

“We will continue to work closely with the government to protect our people and to take steps to keep Americans safe,” Obama said. “The president is grateful for the leadership and professionalism of the first-responders who have been working tirelessly to stop these attacks.”

That changed Sunday, as his presidential opponent Hillary Clinton also took to the stage in New York City at the UN.
“And now, in the wake of the horrific terrorist attacks in Orlando, Florida, I want to call on Congress to pass new legislation to strengthen our intelligence gathering activities. The U.S. Justice Department is leading the FBI investigation, with the support of U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Jeh Johnson.
The two have been meeting with authorities from the FBI, New York State Police and other agencies.
Meanwhile, the Orlando nightclub shooting has reignited a war in the presidential campaign.

Title: Senate Overrides Obama's Veto Of 9/11 Victims Bill
Summary:
After nine months of debate, the Senate on Wednesday overrode Obama’s veto of a bill to let 9/11 victims sue Saudi Arabia. The decision, though, came a little early, with Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) and Minority Leader Harry Reid (D-Nev.) not yet ready to break from Obama’s view and vote to override. McConnell, who previously called the decision a “mistake,” joined in an effort to override Obama’s veto. Reid opposed the motion to overturn the veto, but as he put it, the Senate needed to “do what is right.”
The vote for a veto override was the culmination of many months of legislative wrangling over JASTA. The Obama administration and a host of conservative lawmakers pushed the bill through the Senate but found it unable to get the 60 votes it needed to overcome a filibuster and end the bill’s legislative deadlock.
The Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act was originally expected to clear the Senate in January. It became law, with Obama’s signature and then-Senator Obama signing it over to House leaders, who sent it back for a re-vote. With no Republican backing it, the bill failed in the Senate on Wednesday.
After days of fighting, Obama’s veto was overridden by two Republican members of the Senate, Cornyn and Ted Cruz (Texas).
“There are no excuses,” Obama’s spokesman Ben LaHood said at a Thursday press briefing. “There were no options on either side.”
Obama was the lone dissent in the Senate vote. Other lawmakers took the unusual step of casting their votes for the bill, which will now be signed by the president into law.
The House also took action. It voted to override the Obama veto Wednesday, with the bill becoming law.

Title: Senate Overrides Obama's Veto Of 9/11 Victims Bill
Summary:
The Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act (JASTA) is a controversial bill that seeks to bar foreign government entities from taking part in lawsuits brought by U.S. citizens against foreign governments accused of involvement in terrorist acts. Supporters say it will force the administration of President Barack Obama to take a hardline stance against those accused by victims of terrorism of involvement in their own crimes, while opponents say it would encourage litigation against the accused countries and raise costs for the government in the courts by eliminating sovereign immunity.
What the veto does:
Obama’s initial veto of the bill, which is called “Terrorism Relief and Authorization Act” (H.R. 2063) on the Senate Floor was overridden by more than 99 votes.
A veto override requires a two-thirds majority in the Senate. It also requires an affirmative vote by the House of Representatives. If two-thirds of the House of Representatives vote in favor of the veto override, they send the bill to the president, who must send the bill to the president of the Senate for a second override vote, which is a majority in that chamber.
The bill originally passed the House and Senate without a single “no” vote. Instead, the House and Senate were evenly divided on whether to pass the bill after amendments to it were introduced. The final tally was 97-1 for the House and 97-1 for the Senate.
The bill would allow a United States Court of Appeals to review claims against foreign state entities who allegedly played a role in the attack on New York City’s World Trade Center in 2001. In 2006 the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that foreign government entities couldn’t be sued for acts they may not have performed. As a result of that ruling, many international human rights organizations including Amnesty International have denounced the bill as “unlawful.”
Senators Ted Kennedy (D-Mass.) and Robert Menendez (D-N.J.) spearheaded the bill’s passage through the Senate, with Kennedy being the key vote to overcome Obama’s veto and get the bill passed.
“We all believe that this is a flawed measure,” Kennedy said after the vote on the bill Wednesday. “The president is wrong to put the U.S. in this position to sue foreign governments in this country.”

Title: Senate Overrides Obama's Veto Of 9/11 Victims Bill
Summary:
The Senate had 97 votes to overturn Obama’s veto of the 9/11 bill.
HuffPost’s Mark Berman and Sarah Jones had the story:
It is the first time Congress has had the votes to overrule Obama on a veto. The Senate voted to override Obama’s veto last week, meaning the president’s veto would have become law today.
It took the Senate two days to pass the bill, which could now make its way to the House for a similar vote, and only a handful of senators — including Democrat Chuck Schumer of New York — had even enough votes to override the veto.
The vote was close, with Republicans holding the edge.
At the same time, Democrats were lining up to oppose the veto, with a host of lawmakers who could be voted out of office if the bill ever makes it to the House: former Sens. Russ Feingold of Wisconsin, Evan Bayh of Indiana, Joe Lieberman of Connecticut and Dick Durbin of Illinois.
Sens. John McCain of Arizona, Mike Lee of Utah, Pat Toomey of Pennsylvania, Ron Johnson of Wisconsin and Ben Cardin of Maryland also voted to kill the veto on a bipartisan basis.
The bill’s author, Sen. Richard Burr (R-N.C.), said at a press conference Wednesday that the vote was “a testament to the strength of the American people.”
The bill passed by unanimous consent, clearing the way for a future vote.

Summary:
This morning the Senate confirmed John Brennan as the director of the Terrorist Screening Center and John Brennan, the former deputy director of the CIA, became an associate administrator for the National Security Council, according to the Associated Press, which first reported the news.
The White House did not provide details on the new position. It also did not provide details on the new position's salary. Brennan's salary is expected to be between $275,000 and $355,000 a year, according to the AP, though a spokesperson told the AP the information on his salary was not yet available.
Brennan began his new position in July. Brennan left the CIA in December, after 17 months on the job. He was the first deputy director of the CIA, the agency's director from June 2003 to December 2007.
According to the AP, Brennan replaces David Cohen, who held the new post for nearly a year before leaving in August. Cohen had been serving as the senior vice chief for operations for the CIA. Cohen has held the position since January 2013, and took the post when Cohen left.
Brennan previously served in an administrative capacity in the Office of Special Plans under Leon Panetta, who was then the CIA Director.
The CIA's Office of Inspector General is conducting an extensive review of the agency's oversight of the screening and investigation of foreign intelligence threats at the FBI's counterterrorism center, which is located inside the National Security Operations Center in downtown Washington, D.C., the AP reported.
The review will look at what kinds of changes need to be made at the intelligence center and who should be involved in those changes, the AP reported.
The Senate Judiciary Committee will hold a hearing to consider Brennan's nomination next Wednesday, the AP reported.
On Monday, the House of Representatives approved a bill to pay tribute to the Sept. 11 victims, the latest in a number of bipartisan bills to do so. The bill passed 228-193.

Nancy Pelosi won a resounding re-election victory over Representative Tim Ryan in the race for House Democratic leader Tuesday. Though Democrats had been widely expected to defeat Mr. Ryan in the election, Mr. Ryan had insisted he would run against Ms. Pelosi in his own bid to win back the House’s No. 2 position.
